title: Tagline #003
phrase: Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn

questions.subject: Geography
questions.prompt: Coca-Cola, CNN and the 1996 Summer Olympics call which city home?
questions.factoid: The city's original name was 'Terminus' — literally the end of the railroad line.
questions.connectionNote: The story's beating heart — and its most famous scene is the city burning.

questions.subject: Movies
questions.prompt: Ruby slippers, a yellow brick road and flying monkeys — which 1939 film?
questions.factoid: The ruby slippers were silver in the book — MGM changed them to show off Technicolor.
questions.connectionNote: The lateral link: Victor Fleming walked off The Wizard of Oz mid-production to take over this film — and directed both of 1939's twin monuments.

questions.subject: Old Hollywood
questions.prompt: 'The King of Hollywood' won his only Oscar for It Happened One Night — who was he?
questions.factoid: His Oscar sold at auction in 1996 — Steven Spielberg bought it and donated it back to the Academy.
questions.connectionNote: Gable is Rhett Butler — the man who delivers the line and walks into the fog.

questions.subject: The Oscars
questions.prompt: Who was the first Black performer to win an Academy Award?
questions.factoid: Her Oscar plaque, left to Howard University, vanished decades ago and has never been found.
questions.connectionNote: She won it in 1940 for playing Mammy — at a ceremony held in a segregated hotel she had to get special permission to enter.

questions.subject: Books
questions.prompt: Which Atlanta journalist wrote exactly one novel — and won the Pulitzer Prize for it?
questions.factoid: She wrote the final chapter first and worked backwards toward the beginning.
questions.connectionNote: One book, published 1936. She never wrote another — she never needed to.

reveal.summary: Gone with the Wind. A city, a rival masterpiece, a king, a barrier-breaking Oscar and a one-novel author — every answer orbits the same epic: Atlanta burning, Victor Fleming arriving straight from Oz to direct it, Clark Gable's exit line, Hattie McDaniel's historic win, and Margaret Mitchell's only book. Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn.
reveal.ohMoment: The line almost didn't survive: 'damn' ran afoul of the Production Code, and the studio seriously considered 'Frankly, my dear, I don't care.' The censors blinked — and the American Film Institute later crowned the original the greatest movie quote of all time.

editorial.notes: Canonical-phrase rule applied: trimmed to the exact famous form (no trailing 'about it'), because players type from memory. ONE-TIGHT-ANCHOR RULE: only Atlanta comes from inside the story; the other four answers connect laterally (shared director, cast, Oscar history, authorship) so the theme doesn't announce itself by question two. Letter curve: R(2) → E(2) → N(3) → D(3) → A(4); full success reveals 14 of 27 letters (52%).
